title: ea, i_e and igh
overview:
New spellings: ea, i_e, igh.
No new sound again. More spellings for long e and long i.
Two letters. One sound.
Do not sound them out one by one.
functions: Say the sound for each new spelling
Read a word that has one in it
Write a word that has one in it
Know where in a word each one goes
Read the new words out loud
Choose between two spellings of one sound
learningPath: Words: the new spellings and the new words.
Write the words from their sounds.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
lectureScript:
This is Unit 16. More spellings, no new sounds.
First, long e. You know it as ee.
Feet. Week. That is the sound.
Here is another way to write it. Ea.
Eat. ea. t. Two sounds.
Dream. d. r. ea. m. Four sounds.
Ee and ea are the same sound.
One difference is worth knowing.
Ea can start a word. Eat. Each. Ear.
Ee almost never does.
Now long i. You know it as ie.
Pie. Tie. That is the sound.
Here are two more ways.
The first is i_e. The silent e again.
Pin. Now add an e. Pine.
The e reaches back and makes the i long.
Time. t. i_e. m. Three sounds.
Five. f. i_e. v. Three sounds.
The second is igh. Three letters.
Night. n. igh. t. Three sounds.
Three letters, one sound. That is new.
Light. Right. Might. All the same.
One more thing, and it is useful.
The letter y at the end of a word.
You met y saying its own sound. Yes.
At the END it does something else.
My. Try. Fly. Dry. Why.
It says the long i.
So now long i has four spellings.
Ie in pie. I_e in time. Igh in night. Y in my.
Four ways, one sound. That is English.
That is Unit 16.

grammar.title: The new spellings: ea, i_e, igh
grammar.explanation:
Still no new sounds.
Long e you had as ee. Long i you had as ie.
These are three more ways to write them.
grammar.rule:
ea    as in eat     ea - t
i_e   as in time    t - i_e - m
igh   as in night   n - igh - t

ea is long e. i_e and igh are long i.
grammar.workedExample:
You see ea in a word.
1. Do not read two letters.
2. Read one sound.
3. Say that sound out loud.
4. Now find it in eat.
5. Say the sound again there.
grammar.mistake:
Sounding out both letters gives no word at all.
eat is not e - a - t.
It is ea - t.
grammar.tip: Two letters. Look once. Say once.
grammar.practice:
Say the sound for each one.
1. ea
2. i_e
3. igh
grammar.answers:
Check yourself out loud.
Did you say ONE sound each time?
Two sounds means you read the letters, not the spelling.

grammar.title: Reading a word that has ea, i_e, igh in it
grammar.explanation:
Find the two letters first.
Read them as one sound.
Then read the rest of the word.
grammar.rule:
eat      ea - t
dream    d - r - ea - m
time     t - i_e - m
night    n - igh - t
my       m - y
try      t - r - y
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word dream.
1. Look for the two letters.
2. Cover them with your finger.
3. Read what is left.
4. Now put the one sound back in.
5. Join it all. dream.
grammar.mistake:
Reading left to right, letter by letter, breaks here.
Look for the pair BEFORE you start.
grammar.practice:
Join the sounds and write the word.
1. ea - t
2. d - r - ea - m
3. t - i_e - m
4. n - igh - t
5. m - y
6. t - r - y
grammar.answers:
1. eat
2. dream
3. time
4. night
5. my
6. try
Five or six right? You can read these.

grammar.title: Writing a word that has ea, i_e, igh in it
grammar.explanation:
Say the word. Break it into sounds.
One of those sounds needs TWO letters.
Count sounds, then write.
grammar.rule:
eat      ea - t             2 sounds, 3 letters
dream    d - r - ea - m     4 sounds, 5 letters
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write time.
1. Say it out loud.
2. Break it: t - i_e - m.
3. Which sound needs two letters?
4. Write that pair together.
5. Read it back to check.
grammar.mistake:
One letter for each sound is wrong now.
The new sound takes two letters.
grammar.tip: Count sounds. Some need two letters.
grammar.practice:
Write the word you hear.
1. time
2. night
3. my
4. try
5. five
6. light
grammar.answers:
1. time
2. night
3. my
4. try
5. five
6. light
Five or six right? Good.

grammar.title: y at the end says long i
grammar.explanation:
You met y as a sound of its own. Yes.
At the END of a word it changes.
There it is a vowel, and it says long i.
grammar.rule:
y at the start   yes, yet, yard      its own sound
y at the end     my, try, fly, dry   long i

Same letter. Two jobs.
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word why.
1. Look at where the y is.
2. It is at the end.
3. So it is a vowel here.
4. It says long i.
5. wh - y. Why.
grammar.mistake:
A final y read as its own sound gives nothing.
Muh-yuh is not a word. My is.
grammar.tip: y at the start is a sound. At the end it is a vowel.
grammar.practice:
Say each word. Is the y a sound or a vowel?
1. yes
2. my
3. yard
4. try
5. yet
6. dry
grammar.answers:
1. sound
2. vowel
3. sound
4. vowel
5. sound
6. vowel
The vowels are all at the end. That is the whole rule.

grammar.title: Four ways to write long i
grammar.explanation:
Long i has four spellings.
That is more than any other sound so far.
Position helps with two of them.
grammar.rule:
ie    pie, tie, lie        short words, at the end
i_e   time, five, fine     middle, with silent e
igh   night, light, right  middle, before t
y     my, try, dry         at the end
grammar.workedExample:
You want to read the word sight.
1. Find the pair, or the three.
2. There is igh in the middle.
3. That is one sound. Long i.
4. s - igh - t.
5. Sight.
grammar.mistake:
Reading igh letter by letter gives nothing.
The g and the h are silent. Three letters, one sound.
grammar.tip: igh nearly always comes before t.
grammar.practice:
Which spelling of long i? Write ie, i_e, igh or y.
1. p__
2. t_m_
3. n__t
4. m_
5. f_v_
6. l__t
grammar.answers:
1. pie (ie)
2. time (i_e)
3. night (igh)
4. my (y)
5. five (i_e)
6. light (igh)
Four or more right: you know the shapes.

readings.setting: The wall card, fifteenth one along
readings.passage:

Find a word with ea in it.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The new sounds
speaking.instructions:
Listen and repeat each sound.
ea
i_e
igh
ONE sound each. Not two.
Now say each one three times.
Tap the mic. Say them all.
Check: one sound, or did two slip out?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say one of the new sounds. Say it back.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Read the words
speaking.instructions:
Say each word two ways. Slow, then fast.
1. ea - t ... eat
2. d - r - ea - m ... dream
3. t - i_e - m ... time
4. n - igh - t ... night
5. m - y ... my
6. t - r - y ... try
Tap the mic. Say all six both ways.
Check: was the new spelling one sound?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say three sounds. Join them and say the word.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Say it, then write it
speaking.instructions:
For each word: say it, break it, write it.
1. time
2. night
3. my
4. try
5. five
6. light
Tap the mic. Say each word and its sounds.
Check: did you say the sounds before you wrote?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word with the new spelling. Break it out loud.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Read the list
speaking.instructions:
Read these out loud, straight down the list.
eat
dream
time
night
my
try
five
light
Do it twice. The second time, try not to stop.
Tap the mic. Read the list twice.
Check: was the second time easier?
speaking.tutor: Read the list to the tutor. Ask which words were not clear.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — y at the start, y at the end
speaking.instructions:
Say each word. Then say sound or vowel.
yes. my. yard. try. yet. dry.
At the start it is a sound. At the end it is a vowel.
Tap the mic. Do all six.
Check: were the vowels all at the end?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word that ends in y.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Four ways, one sound
speaking.instructions:
Read these four words, one after the other.
pie. time. night. my.
Four spellings. The same middle sound.
Say the word, then say its spelling.
Tap the mic. Do all four.
Check: did they all have the same vowel sound?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word with igh in it.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Words with the new spelling
writing.prompt:
Say each word. Break it into sounds.
Write two letters for the new sound.
writing.criteria:
Six words.
The new spelling written as a pair.
You read each one back after writing it.
writing.extension: Now write one more word with the same spelling.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Sounds and letters
writing.prompt:
Write each word. Then write two numbers.
How many sounds. How many letters.
writing.criteria:
Six words.
Two numbers beside each one.
The numbers are not the same. That is the point.
writing.extension: Find a word where they ARE the same.

activities.instructions:
Read this list out loud, twice.
eat
dream
time
night
my
try
five
light
activities.answers:
There is no written key.
Check: did you read all eight?
Was the second reading faster than the first?
Stopping on a word is normal. Try again and move on.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Which long i?
activities.instructions:
Fill the gap with ie, i_e, igh or y.
1. p__
2. t_m_
3. n__t
4. m_
5. f_v_
6. l__t
activities.answers:
1. pie
2. time
3. night
4. my
5. five
6. light
Four or more right: you know the shapes.
Below four: igh comes before t. y comes at the end.

quizzes.q: When you see ea you should ___.
quizzes.why: Read the pair as one, not as two letters.

quizzes.q: Join the sounds: ea - t. The word is ___.
quizzes.why: The sounds in order make the word.

quizzes.q: Join the sounds: d - r - ea - m. The word is ___.
quizzes.why: Find the pair first, then read the rest.

quizzes.q: To write a word with the new spelling you ___.
options: write two letters for that sound
write one letter for each sound
quizzes.a: write two letters for that sound
quizzes.why: The new sound is one sound and two letters.

quizzes.q: How many sounds are in night?
quizzes.why: Count what you HEAR. There are more letters than sounds.

options: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.a: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.why: Letter by letter is the slow way here.

quizzes.q: You cannot read a word. What do you do first?
quizzes.why: Find the pair, then read around it.

quizzes.q: At the end of a word, the letter y says ___.
quizzes.why: My, try and dry all end in long i.

quizzes.q: In the word yes, the y is ___.
quizzes.why: At the start it keeps its own sound.

quizzes.q: How many spellings does long i have so far?
quizzes.why: ie, i_e, igh and y at the end.

quizzes.q: The three letters igh make ___ sound.
quizzes.why: The g and the h are silent.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

This is the whole unit, and it goes against everything Units 2 to 7 taught. Expect a learner to read the letters separately for a while. Do not explain it again; point at the pair and say the one sound, and have them say it back. It is a habit, and habits are built by repetition, not by argument.

teacherNotes.type: Find the pair before reading, not during
teacherNotes.note: Left-to-right letter-by-letter reading breaks on these words, because the learner commits to the first letter's sound before they have seen the second. The move is to scan the word for the pair first. A finger under the pair is enough. It looks like a crutch and it is the skill.

From here to the end of the level there are always more letters than sounds. A learner who counts letters will write a spare letter into every word. Have them say the word and count on their fingers before they write.

teacherNotes.type: ea can start a word and ee cannot
teacherNotes.note: This is the one usable difference between the two spellings of long e, and it is worth naming because learners ask. Eat, each, ear, easy. There is no ee word that starts that way. Beyond it, the choice has to be seen.

teacherNotes.type: y is the letter that changes job
teacherNotes.note: It is a consonant at the start and a vowel at the end, and both are common. A learner who has only met yes will read my as muh-yuh and get nothing. The position is the whole rule and it is reliable, which makes this one of the few places in Book B where the answer really is a rule.

teacherNotes.type: igh looks worse than it is
teacherNotes.note: Three letters for one sound alarms people. Say that the g and h are silent, that it nearly always sits before a t, and that there are perhaps twenty common words with it. Night, light, right, might, sight, fight, bright, tight. Read the list once and most of them are done.

assignment.title: Read and write the new words
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Record yourself. Say the sound for each new spelling.
Then read these words, slowly and then faster:
eat, dream, time, night, my, try
2. Write six of the words from their sounds.
Beside each one, write how many sounds it has.
Listen back before you finish.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written page
